rejected.title: Social and emotional wellbeing
card: Social and emotional wellbeing is a holistic view of health held by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Holistic means the whole person and their connections are considered together, not as separate parts.
It links body and mind with family, community, culture, Country and spirituality. Country means the land, waters and sky that a people belong to and care for.
Because these parts are linked, a problem in one can affect the others. For example, being cut off from Country or community may affect a person's mental wellbeing.

This differs from a view that treats mental health mainly as something inside an individual. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and communities have their own understandings of wellbeing, which should be respected.
rejected.remember: Social and emotional wellbeing is whole-person: body, mind and connections to people, culture and Country.

a.q: Which description best fits social and emotional wellbeing?
opts: A view linking the person to family, culture and Country
A view focused on the absence of mental illness in a person
A view where body and mind are treated as separate systems
A view based mainly on a person's individual coping skills
a.why: Social and emotional wellbeing is holistic, so it joins body and mind with family, community, culture, Country and spirituality. The option about absence of illness is tempting, but it looks only at the individual and leaves out these connections.
a.clue: Think about what the word holistic includes.

b.q: Uncle Ray is an Aboriginal man who moved to a city far from his Country and family. He feels low and disconnected. Which explanation fits a social and emotional wellbeing view?
opts: Losing links to Country and kin can affect his wellbeing
His low mood is caused by a problem in his brain alone
His feelings have nothing to do with family or Country
Only his physical health matters for his overall wellbeing
b.why: This view treats wellbeing as linked to family, community and Country, so losing those connections can affect how a person feels. The brain-only option is tempting, but it treats the person as separate from their connections, which this view does not do.
b.clue: Which option keeps the person connected to Country and family?

version.title: Social and emotional wellbeing
card: Social and emotional wellbeing is a holistic view of health held by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Holistic means the whole person and their connections are seen together.
It links body and mind with family and kin, community, culture, Country and spirituality. Country means the land, waters and skies a people belong to and care for.
These parts are connected, so strength or harm in one can flow to the others. Strong ties to family and culture can support wellbeing.
This differs from views that treat mental health mainly as something inside one person. Different communities hold their own understandings of wellbeing.
version.remember: Wellbeing is the whole person in connection: body, mind, kin, community, culture, Country and spirit.

a.q: How does a social and emotional wellbeing view differ from a view of mental health focused on the individual?
opts: It sees wellbeing through a person's connections
It looks only at whether illness is present
It treats body and mind as separate systems
It rests mainly on a person's own coping skills
a.why: Social and emotional wellbeing is holistic: it sees a person through their links to family, community, culture, Country and spirituality. Looking only at illness, or at one person's coping, is closer to an individual view.

b.q: A community health service in Victoria wants to support the social and emotional wellbeing of Aboriginal young people. Which approach best fits this view?
opts: Include family, culture and time on Country
Treat each young person's mind on its own
Treat physical health as a separate issue
Measure wellbeing by test results at school
b.why: Social and emotional wellbeing joins body and mind with family, community, culture, Country and spirituality, so support draws on those connections. Treating the mind on its own, or the body apart, leaves those connections out.
b.clue: Which approach keeps the young person's connections in view?

a.best: It sees wellbeing through a person's connections

b.best: Include family, culture and time on Country
